topic: Would you let an always-on AI agent email your client?

slides.title: Let an AI email your *client*?
slides.sub: OpenAI's Dots just launched. Claude and Grok are in the same race. Here's the rule I'd use.

slides.title: OpenAI just shipped always-on agents
slides.body: Dots work between your chats. Each gets its own cloud computer and plugs into 4,000+ apps like Slack. Work comes back for you to review.
slides.source: Source: OpenAI DevDay launch, Sept 29 2026, as reported by TechCrunch and 9to5Google.

slides.title: Clients judge your response time
slides.body: Nobody sees your tools. They see how fast you answer, and whether the answer comes with a reason.
slides.fix: An agent that has the answer before the question lands.

slides.title: Three agents, three bets
items: Dots: always on, works between chats
Claude Code: you stay in the loop
Grok Build: parallel agents, early beta
slides.body: Early reviews split on benchmarks. Pick by how much control you want, not by a leaderboard.

slides.title: Agents draft. Humans send.
slides.body: My rule from building these: anything that leaves the building gets a human's eyes first. Clients remember the one bad email.
slides.fix: Let the agent do the work. Keep the send button.

slides.title: Would you phone them about it?
slides.body: If you'd phone the client, don't let an agent write it. If you'd send the same note to 40 clients, automate it.
slides.fix: Bad news, pricing, apologies: you. Reports, reminders, status updates: agent drafts.

slides.title: My Monday report builds itself
slides.body: campaign-report-autopilot assembles the client report every Monday on GitHub Actions, with scale, keep, test and cut calls. A human still approves what leaves.

slides.title: What I'd hand over
slides.source: Your line may sit somewhere else. That's the interesting part.

slides.title: Where's your line?
slides.sub: Would you let an agent email a client? Say yes, no, or drafts only.

caption: OpenAI just shipped Dots: agents that work between your chats.
Claude and Grok are in the same race.
Every one of them promises "it does it for you."
Here's my filter for client work:
→ Reports, reminders, status: agent drafts
→ Spikes and anomalies: agent flags
→ Bad news, pricing, renewals: you
→ Anything that leaves the building: a human reads it first
The bad-news test:
If you'd phone the client, don't let an agent write it.
If you'd send the same note to 40 clients, automate it.
I'd rather be the account manager who had the answer at 6am than the one who heard about it at 9:02.
Source: TechCrunch and 9to5Google, Sept 29 2026.
